newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, New Caledonia nearer pact on island future.
newsitem.headline: France, New Caledonia nearer pact on island future.

text.p: The French government and officials of the two main political parties of the French South Pacific island of New Caledonia reported progress on Thursday in a new round of talks aimed at resolving the island's future status.

"The three partners consider these talks could well lead to a voluntary initiative leading to a negotiated solution for the territory's future," the three parties said in a joint statement issued at the close of four days of talks.

In one key breakthrough, the parties agreed to proceed with a French proposal to reallocate mining reserves within the territory so that local Kanak independence groups could go ahead with a plan to build a nickel plant in northern New Caledonia.
That proposal involves a swap of the mining titles of the island's Koniambo field with those of the Poum field, so that Koniambo reserves can be used to supply the planned nickel plant.
The Koniambo field belongs to Eramet, a nickel producer that is majority-owned by France.
"The prime minister assured his Caledonian partners that he would do all that he could to facilitate the rapid conclusion of this agreement," the joint statement said.
Rock Wamytan, president of the pro-independence Kanak Socialist National Liberation Front party (FLNKS), told reporters the swap proposal was still "at a preliminary stage".
"But the state has confirmed through the prime minister's voice its willingness to do all in its power to resolve this problem in the coming days," Wamytan said.
The other party participating in the talks was the anti- independence Rally for a Republican Caledonia, allied with President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist Rally for the Republic.

Officials said Paris planned to send Overseas Territories Minister Jean-Jacques de Peretti to New Caledonia next month to wrap up the nickel swap deal and press on with the talks aimed at resolving the island's future relationship with France.
The goal was to settle that issue prior to 1998 general elections in France, the parties said.
Negotiations collapsed in April 1996 after divisions broke out among the members of the FLNKS delegation.

France hopes an agreement on greater autonomy for the territory could head off a tricky referendum on self- determination set for 1998 under a 1988 agreement which ended violence on the island of 170,000 people that is 18,000 km (11,000 miles) from mainland France.
